claims.text: Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi is a single-phase FCC alloy.
The equiatomic quinary alloy deforms through a synergistic sequence involving dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
Reducing the number of constituents in CrMnFeCoNi-derived FCC alloys decreases local chemical heterogeneity.
Reducing the number of constituents decreases the degree or spatial variation of short-range chemical order.
Local chemical order governs spatial variations in local stacking-fault energy.
Variation in local chemical order can alter the selection among extended dislocations, stacking faults, deformation twinning, and other deformation modes.
Lower compositional complexity produces a more uniform local atomic environment.
A more uniform local atomic environment reduces fluctuations in stacking-fault energy.
Reduced stacking-fault-energy fluctuations raise the effective barrier for deformation-twin nucleation.
A higher effective twin-nucleation barrier diminishes deformation twinning.
Quaternary and ternary derivatives shift from slip-plus-twinning plasticity toward predominantly dislocation-mediated slip.
Quaternary and especially ternary derivatives will have lower deformation-twin density than the quinary baseline.
Quaternary and ternary derivatives will have lower strain-hardening rates than the quinary baseline.
Reduced twin-assisted plasticity will reduce overall ductility and toughness in the quaternary and ternary derivatives.
Reduced dynamic accommodation may give the quaternary and ternary derivatives somewhat higher initial yield strengths.
Differences in processing can change local chemical order at fixed overall composition and thereby change strength, strain hardening, ductility, and the preferred deformation modes.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase FCC solid solutions tested without secondary-phase formation or unrelated deformation-induced phase transformations.
